paras: The Kinston jail lynching plot was a reported plan in early August 1920 by a group of a score or more people to kill three Black prisoners held in the county jail at Kinston, North Carolina, before they could be tried. Officials moved one of the men, Joseph Franklin, out of the county and on to Raleigh, and no one was reported harmed. The story reached readers only through a Black wire dispatch, which Black weeklies headlined as a lynching attempt that had been balked or "outwitted".

Three Black men, described as "three Colored men" or "three Negroes", were held in the county jail at Kinston, at least one of them on a charge of attempted criminal assault. The dispatch names them as Joseph Franklin, a man called only Aldridge, and James Jackson, but does not say which of them faced the assault charge. On the little evidence they had, the authorities at first thought the charge exaggerated and expected no trouble.

According to the dispatch, it was later "admitted at the court house" that a score or more people had planned "saving the state the trouble of trying" the three prisoners. The authorities did not know of the plot at the time, but their views "were changed suddenly" when they came to believe that summary vengeance on one of the men was planned. They hurried Franklin to another county, whose officials declined to receive him, and from there took him to Raleigh.

Officials had heard that Aldridge was also "to be included in the job" to make it "a good one". Summary action against James Jackson "would have been folly", the dispatch said, because officers were not certain he was the right man. Jackson was also said to be suffering serious effects from a silver plate in his head that had slipped out of place.
No report of arrests among the plotters, of a trial of the three prisoners, or of their later fate appears in the coverage.

All known coverage came from one dispatch, which the Richmond Planet credited to the Associated Negro Press and which ran in four Black weeklies between August 6 and August 14, 1920. The Cleveland Advocate placed it on its front page under the headline "Authorities Balk Lynching Attempt", crediting officials with preventing the killing. The Richmond Planet went further with "Mob Outwitted in Attempt to Lynch Innocent Man", turning the officers' doubts about Jackson into a claim of innocence that the text itself did not make.

The Black Dispatch and the Savannah Tribune printed the same text without a headline of their own, among other short dispatches. The copies differ on the date: the Cleveland Advocate dated the Kinston dispatch August 5, the Savannah Tribune "Aug 4th", and the Richmond Planet only "August". No report of the plot in white newspapers appears in the coverage examined.

reader.title: Kinston jail lynching plot (1920)
bases: A wire story reported that a group of a score or more planned to kill three Black prisoners held in the county jail before trial, and that officials moved one of them away (A2, A3, A4).

A group of 'a score or more' reportedly planned to save 'the state the trouble of trying' three jailed men on a charge of attempted criminal assault, which fits a lynching pretext, but no one was reported killed or even seized; it was a threatened lynching (A2, A3, A4).
All four copies print one wire story (credited to the Associated Negro Press in A3) with no independent local or white-press report (A1, A2, A3, A4).

accounts.label: Wire report (Kinston dateline, Associated Negro Press)
accounts.gist: A score or more persons planned to kill three jailed Black men; the authorities moved Joseph Franklin away to Raleigh after another county refused him, and officers doubted Jackson was the right man.

framing.detail: The Cleveland Advocate ran the wire text on its front page under 'AUTHORITIES BALK LYNCHING ATTEMPT'.
The Richmond Planet headlined it 'MOB OUTWITTED IN ATTEMPT TO LYNCH INNOCENT MAN', drawing on the officers' doubt about Jackson's guilt.
The Black Dispatch and the Savannah Tribune ran the text without comment among other dispatches.

conflicts.note: The datelines are the date of the dispatch, not necessarily of the plot or the removal of Franklin; the Black Dispatch printed the item on August 6, so the dispatch was filed by then (A1).
